name: HTML & CSS
author: Recurse
subject: web
description: Structure pages with semantic, accessible HTML and lay them out with CSS, flexbox, grid and media queries.

lesson.intro: HTML describes what the content of a page is, and CSS describes how it looks. This lesson covers page structure, semantic and accessible markup, forms, how CSS decides which rule wins, the box model, flexbox and grid, and making a layout adapt to any screen.

sections.title: Document structure and semantic HTML
sections.body:
Every page has the same skeleton. `<!DOCTYPE html>` tells the browser to use modern standards mode. Inside `<html lang="en">`, the `<head>` holds information about the page, such as the character set, the title shown in the browser tab and links to stylesheets. The `<body>` holds what is shown.

Semantic elements say what content is, not how it looks:
- `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>` and `<footer>` mark the regions of a page. Use one `<main>` per page for its primary content.
- `<article>` is self-contained content such as a blog post; `<section>` groups related content under a heading.
- Headings `<h1>` to `<h6>` form an outline. Do not skip levels to get a smaller font; change the size with CSS.

Screen readers, search engines and browser features all rely on these meanings. A screen reader user can jump straight between headings, landmarks such as `<nav>` and `<main>`, and form fields.

Accessibility basics:
- Give every meaningful image an `alt` that says what it shows. Use `alt=""` for purely decorative images so screen readers skip them.
- Use `<button>` for actions and `<a href>` for navigation. A `<div>` with a click handler cannot be reached with Tab or pressed with Enter unless you rebuild all of that yourself.

sections.tip: Try navigating your page with only the Tab and Enter keys. Anything you cannot reach is a problem for keyboard users.

check.question: Which `alt` value is right for a decorative divider image that adds no information?
choices: alt="image"
alt=""
alt="decorative divider image"
No alt attribute at all
check.explanation: An empty alt tells screen readers to skip the image. Leaving alt out entirely makes many screen readers read the file name instead.

sections.title: Forms and labels
sections.body:
A `<form>` collects input and sends it to the URL in `action`, using the HTTP method in `method`. With `method="get"` the fields are added to the URL as a query string; use `method="post"` for anything that changes data or contains private information.

- Each field's `name` becomes its key in the submitted data. A field without a `name` is not submitted at all.
- Every field needs a visible `<label>`. Link them by giving the label a `for` that matches the input's `id`, or wrap the input inside the label. Clicking the label then focuses the field, and screen readers announce the label as the field's name.
- A `placeholder` is a hint that disappears as soon as the user types. It does not replace a label.
- Types such as `email`, `number`, `date` and `password` bring the right keyboard on phones and built-in checks. `required` stops the form from submitting while the field is empty.
- A `<button>` inside a form submits it by default. Give buttons that should not submit `type="button"`.
sections.code:
<form action="/signup" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>

  <label>
    <input name="newsletter" type="checkbox"> Send me the newsletter
  </label>

  <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
</form>
sections.tip: Group related radio buttons or checkboxes in a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>` that asks the question.

check.question: A form submits, but the server never receives the phone number. The field is `<input id="phone" type="tel">`. What is missing?
choices: A placeholder
A label
type="number"
A name attribute
check.explanation: Only fields with a name are included in the submitted data. The id links the field to its label but is not sent.

sections.title: Selectors, specificity and the box model
sections.body:
A CSS rule is a selector plus declarations: `p { color: gray; }`. Common selectors:
- `p` (type), `.card` (class), `#main` (id), `[type="email"]` (attribute)
- `nav a` matches any `a` inside a `nav`; `ul > li` matches only direct children
- `a:hover` and `li:first-child` are pseudo-classes

When several rules set the same property on an element, the cascade picks one. `!important` declarations win first. Otherwise the more specific selector wins, and if specificity ties, the rule that comes later wins.

Specificity is compared as three counts, left to right: ids, then classes, attributes and pseudo-classes, then elements. `#top a` is (1,0,1) and beats `.menu .item a` at (0,2,1), because one id outranks any number of classes. Inline `style` attributes beat every selector.

Every element is a box: the content, then padding, then a border, then margin outside the border. By default (`box-sizing: content-box`) `width` sets only the content, so padding and border are added on top. With `box-sizing: border-box`, `width` includes padding and border, which is easier to reason about.

Vertical margins between blocks collapse: a bottom margin of 20px above a top margin of 30px gives a 30px gap, not 50px.
sections.tip: Your browser's developer tools show the box model of any element and list which rules were overridden.

check.question: Two rules have exactly the same specificity and both set `color` on a paragraph. Which one wins?
choices: The one that comes later in the CSS
The one that comes first in the CSS
The one with the shorter selector
Neither; the browser falls back to the default color
check.explanation: When importance and specificity tie, source order decides and the last declaration wins.

sections.title: Flexbox and grid
sections.body:
Flexbox lays out items in one direction, a row or a column. Put `display: flex` on the container, and its direct children become flex items.
- `flex-direction` sets the main axis: `row` (the default) or `column`.
- `justify-content` places items along the main axis: `flex-start`, `center`, `space-between`.
- `align-items` places them on the cross axis, which is vertical in a row.
- `gap` adds space between items, and `flex: 1` on an item lets it grow into leftover space.
- `flex-wrap: wrap` lets items move onto a new line instead of shrinking.

Grid lays out items in two dimensions, rows and columns at once. `grid-template-columns` defines the columns, and the `fr` unit means a share of the free space. Items fill the cells in order, and `grid-column: 1 / 3` makes one item run from grid line 1 to line 3, which spans two columns.

A rule of thumb: flexbox for a line of things such as a navbar, toolbar or row of buttons; grid for page layouts and card galleries.
sections.tip: Flex and grid properties only work when the parent has `display: flex` or `display: grid`.

check.question: What does `grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr` create?
choices: Two columns, exactly 1px and 2px wide
Two rows, the second twice as tall as the first
Two columns; the second gets twice the free space
One column, three fractions of the page wide
check.explanation: Each fr value is a share of the available space: 1 + 2 = 3 shares, so the columns get one third and two thirds.

sections.title: Responsive design and media queries
sections.body:
Responsive design means one page that adapts to any screen width.

- Put `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` in the head. Without it, phones lay the page out at a desktop width of about 980px and shrink it, so text is tiny and width-based media queries do not match the real screen.
- Prefer flexible units: `%`, `fr`, `rem` (relative to the root font size) and `max-width` rather than fixed widths. `img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }` stops images from overflowing their container.
- Media queries apply rules only when a condition is true. Mobile-first means writing the base styles for small screens, then adding `min-width` queries for larger ones.

When several media queries match, the normal cascade applies, so a later matching rule overrides an earlier one.
sections.tip: Use the device toolbar in your browser's developer tools to preview a page at phone and tablet widths.

check.question: With the CSS above, how many columns does the gallery have on a screen 800px wide?
check.explanation: 800px matches min-width: 600px but not min-width: 1000px, so the two-column rule overrides the one-column base.

keyTerms.definition: An HTML element that describes the meaning of its content, such as nav, main or article.
The alt attribute of an image: a text alternative read by screen readers, empty for decorative images.
The element that names a form field; linked with for and id, or by wrapping the field.
The weight of a selector, compared as counts of ids, then classes, then elements.
Every element is content plus padding, border and margin, from the inside out.
A box-sizing value where width and height include padding and border.
A grid unit that stands for one share of the free space in the grid container.
A CSS condition, such as min-width: 600px, that applies rules only when it is true.

summary: Use semantic elements and real buttons, links and labels, because assistive technology depends on them.
A form field needs a `name` to be submitted and a `<label>` to be usable.
The cascade picks a winner by importance, then specificity (ids, classes, elements), then source order.
With `box-sizing: border-box`, the width you set includes padding and border.
Flexbox arranges items in one direction, grid in two, and media queries adapt the layout to the screen.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend building their first web page why they should use `<button>` and `<label>` instead of styled `<div>` elements, and how a media query lets the same page work on a phone and a laptop.

questions.question: Why is `<button>` better than `<div onclick="save()">` for a Save action?
choices: Divs cannot have click handlers in modern browsers
Buttons load faster and use less memory than divs
It is keyboard-accessible (Tab, Enter, Space) by default
Only buttons can be styled with CSS hover effects
questions.explanation: Buttons come with keyboard focus, key handling and a role that screen readers announce. A div needs tabindex, a role and key handlers added by hand to match, and is easy to get wrong.

questions.question: Which element should wrap the primary content of a page, and appear only once? Type its tag name.
questions.explanation: <main> marks the central content of the page, so screen reader users can jump straight to it past the header and navigation.

questions.question: An accessibility checker flags this markup. What is the problem?
choices: Headings skip from h1 to h4; use h2 and style it with CSS
A paragraph cannot directly follow a heading element
The h1 must be wrapped inside a header element
Headings need an alt attribute for screen readers
questions.explanation: Headings form an outline, and jumping from h1 to h4 suggests missing levels to people navigating by headings. Pick the level by structure and change the look with CSS.

questions.question: Where does the `<title>` element go, and what does it control?
choices: In the body; it is the main visible heading of the page
In the head; it sets the largest heading shown on the page
In the footer; it labels the page when it is printed
In the head; it sets the text shown in the browser tab
questions.explanation: <title> belongs in <head> and is not shown in the page itself; browsers show it in the tab and search engines use it as the result title. The visible main heading is the <h1>.

questions.question: Complete the label so that clicking it focuses the email input.
choices: for="email"
for="user-email"
name="user-email"
id="user-email"
questions.explanation: A label's for attribute must match the input's id, which is user-email. It is not linked to the name, which is the key used when the form is submitted.

questions.question: A search form uses `method="get"`. Where do the field values end up?
choices: In the URL query string, such as /search?q=lamp
In the request body, hidden from the URL
In a cookie the browser sets for the site
In the page's local storage until submitted
questions.explanation: GET forms put the fields in the query string, which makes results bookmarkable and shareable. That is also why passwords and data-changing forms should use POST.

questions.question: Clicking "Show password" submits the form and reloads the page. Why?
questions.code:
<form action="/login" method="post">
  <label for="pw">Password</label>
  <input id="pw" name="password" type="password">
  <button onclick="togglePassword()">Show password</button>
  <button type="submit">Log in</button>
</form>
choices: onclick cannot be used on buttons that are inside a form
The form needs method="get" for extra buttons to work
Every button in a form submits it, whatever its type is
Buttons in a form default to type="submit"; add type="button"
questions.explanation: A <button> with no type inside a form is a submit button. After togglePassword() runs, the click submits the form. type="button" makes it do nothing except run its handler.

questions.question: Why should every form field have a `<label>`, even when it already has a placeholder?
questions.answer: A label stays visible while the user types, is announced by screen readers as the field's name, and makes its text clickable to focus the field. A placeholder disappears once typing starts and is not a reliable replacement.
questions.explanation: Placeholders are hints. People who are interrupted mid-form, use screen readers, or have memory difficulties rely on a label that stays put.

questions.question: Write the specificity of `#nav .item a` as three numbers for ids, classes and elements, like 0,2,1.
questions.explanation: #nav is one id, .item is one class, and a is one element, giving (1,1,1).

questions.question: What color is the link?
choices: green
blue
red
the browser default
questions.explanation: #top a is (1,0,1), .menu .link is (0,2,0) and a.link is (0,1,1). The id makes #top a the most specific, so source order never comes into play.

questions.question: A box has `width: 200px; padding: 10px; border: 5px solid;` and the default `box-sizing: content-box`. How many pixels wide is it on screen, including the border?
questions.explanation: With content-box, width covers only the content: 200 + 10 + 10 of padding + 5 + 5 of border = 230. With border-box it would be exactly 200.

questions.question: One paragraph has `margin-bottom: 20px` and the paragraph below it has `margin-top: 30px`. How big is the gap between them?
choices: 50px
30px
20px
10px
questions.explanation: Adjacent vertical margins of block elements collapse into one, the size of the larger margin. Horizontal margins never collapse.

questions.question: A flex container has `flex-direction: column`. Which declaration centers its items horizontally?
choices: justify-content: center
text-align: center
vertical-align: middle
align-items: center
questions.explanation: In a column the main axis runs vertically, so justify-content centers items vertically. align-items works on the cross axis, which is now horizontal.

questions.question: Complete the rule so the cards form three equal columns.
choices: repeat(3, 1fr)
3fr
1fr / 3
repeat(1fr, 3)
questions.explanation: repeat(3, 1fr) is shorthand for 1fr 1fr 1fr: three columns sharing the space equally. 3fr alone defines a single column.

questions.question: The links inside .nav should spread out in a row, but justify-content has no effect. Why?
choices: justify-content only works in grid layouts
align-items must come before justify-content
The container is missing display: flex
space-between also needs a gap value
questions.explanation: justify-content and align-items only apply to flex or grid containers. Without display: flex, .nav is a normal block and its children ignore them.

questions.question: Complete the media query so the sidebar is shown only on screens 900px wide or wider.
choices: max-width: 900px
min-width: 900px
width: 900px
min-height: 900px
questions.explanation: min-width: 900px matches when the viewport is at least 900px wide. max-width would do the opposite, and width: 900px matches only at exactly 900px.

questions.question: A page looks tiny and zoomed out on phones, and its `max-width: 600px` media query never applies there. What is most likely missing?
choices: A max-width on the body element
The lang attribute on the html element
A min-width media query for desktops
The viewport meta tag in the head
questions.explanation: Without <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">, mobile browsers lay the page out about 980px wide and scale it down, so the 600px query never matches.
